status_summary: The FTC is acting on children's online protection through COPPA and general Section 5 authority, but no proceeding built on the chapter's contracts-with-minors theory or a written parental consent requirement was found. The amended COPPA Rule, which the FTC topic page lists as finalized on 2025-01-16 before the period tracked, was published 2025-04-22 and its full compliance date passed on 2026-04-22; the sources read describe no change to its under-13 scope, which the chapter criticizes. The FTC ordered seven companies on 2025-09-11 to report on AI companion chatbots and minors, and on 2025-09-29 referred a complaint against the operator of the Sendit app alleging, among other violations, that it unfairly used fake messages to push child and teen users into subscriptions. In 2026 the FTC held an age-verification workshop (2026-01-28) and issued a policy statement (2026-02-25) easing COPPA enforcement for data collected solely to verify age, which responds to the privacy concern the chapter's skeptics raise. On 2026-05-20 the FTC began enforcing the civil provisions of the TAKE IT DOWN Act, a related but distinct child-protection authority. In Congress, the House passed the KIDS Act (H.R. 7757) on 2026-06-29, whose text would raise the COPPA child age to under 14 and add teen protections, and the Senate Commerce Committee ordered the Kids Online Safety Act (S. 1748) reported on 2026-08-05; no enactment was found, and the App Store Accountability Act (H.R. 3149) shows a subcommittee vote on 2025-12-11 as its latest action.

timeline.event: FTC publishes the amended Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule in the Federal Register (effective 2025-06-23; full compliance due 2026-04-22), adding separate parental consent for third-party disclosures, written security and retention requirements and coverage of biometric identifiers; the law-firm summaries read describe no change to the under-13 scope.

FTC issues Section 6(b) orders (vote 3-0) to Alphabet, Character Technologies, Instagram, Meta, OpenAI, Snap and xAI for information on how AI companion chatbots affect children and teens, including age restrictions, parental notice and COPPA compliance.

FTC (vote 3-0) refers to DOJ a complaint against Iconic Hearts Holdings, operator of the Sendit app, and its CEO, alleging COPPA violations (no parental notice or consent), FTC Act violations including unfair use of fake messages to push child and teen users into paid subscriptions, and ROSCA subscription-billing violations; the complaint was filed by DOJ in the Central District of California.
FTC held a public workshop on age verification technologies (date as listed on the FTC kids privacy topic page; the 2026-02-25 FTC release gives the month as January 2026).

FTC (vote 2-0) issues an enforcement policy statement under which it will not bring COPPA Rule actions against general-audience and mixed-audience operators that collect children's data solely to estimate age, without prior parental consent, if conditions on use, retention, sharing, notice, security and accuracy are met; it says it plans to review the COPPA Rule on age verification. The statement remains in effect until final rule amendments are published or it is withdrawn.

FTC begins enforcing the platform notice-and-removal provisions (section 3) of the TAKE IT DOWN Act on nonconsensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated content, under which covered platforms must remove reported content within 48 hours; the week before, the Chairman sent reminder letters to four large technology companies. The act is adjacent to, not the same as, the chapter's unfair-contract theory.

House passes H.R. 7757, the KIDS Act (sponsor Rep. Guthrie), 267-117 (Roll no. 228) on a motion to suspend the rules and pass the bill as amended; the engrossed text includes a Kids Online Safety Act title, a COPPA 2.0 title raising the child age from under 13 to under 14 and covering ages 14 to 17 as teens, and a chatbot title. It was received in the Senate and referred to the Commerce Committee on 2026-07-13.
Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee orders S. 1748, the Kids Online Safety Act, reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
